links.outcome: Stereotyping and linguistic bias in GPT-4 gender-tailored patient education content
links.effect: Revisions occasionally relied on social stereotypes (e.g., 'bottling up emotions'); both versions framed female symptoms as 'atypical' and showed gendered assumptions in recommended activities; 4 of 7 male-tailored revisions omitted erectile dysfunction.
links.quote: Revisions also occasionally relied on social stereotypes (e.g., “bottling up emotions”).

links.outcome: Completeness of clinical content in GPT-4 sex-specific CVD education revisions
links.effect: Male-tailored versions often missed key clinical factors; 4 of 7 revisions failed to mention erectile dysfunction as a CVD risk marker, while female-tailored versions incorporated biological facts such as menopause.
links.quote: For instance, 4 of 7 revisions failed to mention erectile dysfunction as a CVD risk marker.

links.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid Reading Ease) of GPT-4 revised patient education materials
links.effect: Readability was maintained after GPT-4 revision; the gender-inclusivity checklist median rose from 3.0/10 (original) to 8.0 (male-tailored) and 10.0 (female-tailored).

unlisted_practices: Using LLMs with structured prompts to tailor patient education materials by sex/gender

screen.reason: The study evaluates GPT-4's performance and biases when personalizing cardiovascular disease patient education materials for male vs. female audiences. It does not test a specific deployment safeguard or intervention.
